Chapter Ten: The Unfinished Work of Justice
As the years go by and Leopold’s Congo slips further into history, there’s something we can’t ignore—the work of justice isn’t done yet. Those deep wounds from the past? They’re still raw in many ways. And even though times have changed, the old systems of exploitation and inequality? Well, they’ve just slipped into new disguises.
So, what can we do if we care about justice? How do we move beyond just talking and actually make a difference? That’s the challenge—finding real ways to address these heavy legacies, with action, not just words.
Picture this: a group of young activists, inspired by what happened in the Congo Free State, decide they’ve had enough. They come together and launch a campaign—calling for reparations and demanding more transparency from international corporations doing business in the region. Sure, they run into skepticism and pushback. But they don’t back down. They understand that real change is slow, and sometimes the wins are small and fragile. Still, they believe—deep down—that this struggle is absolutely worth it.
Over in Belgium, there’s a new generation looking squarely at their country’s colonial legacy. They’re honest, even humble about it. They’re calling for old statues to come down, for textbooks to tell the truth, and for the nation to finally admit its past mistakes. Of course, not everyone’s on board—some folks cling to comforting old stories. But others see this as a real chance to build a fairer, more inclusive society.
When you really think about it, the work of justice isn’t just about fixing what went wrong in the past. It’s about creating a future where dignity, equality, and truth actually have a place. It’s about listening—really listening—to people whose voices were ignored for too long. And it’s about having the guts to take action, even when it feels like the odds are stacked against you.
The story of King Leopold’s Congo reminds us—history doesn’t have to decide our future. The choices we make, whether as individuals or as a society, they matter. The pursuit of justice is never really finished, but trust me—it’s always worth it.
